questions.question: Which credential does the Datadog Agent require in order to submit metrics and events to Datadog?
choices: An API key
An application key
A client token
A service account token
questions.explanation: Datadog's docs state that an API key is required by the Datadog Agent to submit metrics and events; it is set with `api_key` in datadog.yaml or `DD_API_KEY`. Application keys are used together with an API key for programmatic API access such as reading data, and client tokens are for browser, mobile and TV apps. The Agent does not need a service account credential to send data.

questions.question: In the Agent's main configuration file, `datadog.yaml`, which setting holds the key the Agent uses to send data to Datadog?
choices: `app_key`
`dd_url`
`api_key`
`client_token`
questions.explanation: `api_key` (environment variable `DD_API_KEY`) is marked as required in the example datadog.yaml and is described as the key used by the Agent to submit metrics and events. `app_key` is optional and only gives access to Datadog's programmatic API, `dd_url` overrides the metrics intake host, and client tokens are not an Agent setting.

questions.question: Which statement about Datadog API keys is accurate?
choices: They are unique to an organization, and an org can have several active at once
Each user gets one personal API key that inherits that user's role and permissions
One API key works across every Datadog site, such as both US1 and EU1
They expire automatically 90 days after creation unless they are renewed
questions.explanation: API keys are unique to your organization, and Datadog recommends creating multiple API keys (up to 50 by default) so each can be rotated or revoked on its own. Inheriting a user's permissions describes application keys, not API keys. Datadog sites are completely independent, and API keys are long-lived with no built-in expiration.

questions.question: A front-end team is adding Datadog browser log collection and RUM to a public web app. Which credential should they embed in the JavaScript?
choices: An organization API key
A client token
An application key
An API key plus an application key
questions.explanation: API keys cannot be used to send data from a browser, mobile or TV app because they would be exposed client-side, so end-user-facing applications such as the browser log collector and RUM use client tokens. Application keys grant access to Datadog's programmatic API and must never be exposed in browser code, alone or combined with an API key.

questions.question: By default, what is the maximum number of API keys a Datadog organization can have?
questions.explanation: An org must have at least one API key and can have up to 50 API keys by default; Datadog Support can raise the limit on request. Managed API keys created by a Datadog integration or service don't count toward this limit. 10, 25 and 100 are not the documented default.

questions.question: Your org uses a single API key for Kubernetes Agents in AWS, Chef-managed on-prem Agents and Terraform scripts. Security wants to be able to revoke the Terraform credential without touching any Agents. What should you do?
choices: Replace the Terraform API key with a client token
Create a separate API key for each deployment method
Issue each Agent its own application key instead
Rename the existing API key to mark it as Terraform-only
questions.explanation: Datadog recommends a different API key for each deployment method (for example Kubernetes in AWS, on-prem with Chef, Terraform, local development) so one key can be rotated or revoked without affecting the others. Renaming a key doesn't change its value, client tokens are only for browser, mobile and TV clients, and the Agent submits data with an API key rather than an application key.

questions.question: An API key used by a single test VM was accidentally committed to a public GitHub repository. According to Datadog's guidance, what is the first step?
choices: Delete the file from the GitHub repository
Disable the user account that created the key
Ask Datadog Support to change the key's value
Revoke the exposed key on the API Keys page
questions.explanation: The documented response starts with revoking the affected key, then removing it from public files and commit history, creating a new key, updating services and reviewing the account for unapproved access. Deleting the file alone does not guarantee nobody already copied the key. Disabling the creator does nothing to an API key, because API keys created by a disabled account remain valid.

questions.question: An exposed API key is used by hundreds of Agents across several environments, and nobody is sure where all of them run. What does Datadog advise about when to revoke it?
choices: Revoke it at once and watch which Agents stop reporting data
Create and roll out a new key first, then revoke the exposed one
Leave it active, since API keys can only write data and never read
Revoke it at once; the Agents fall back to their application key
questions.explanation: Revoking an active key can impact your services, so when the scope of usage is large or undetermined Datadog suggests doing the other steps (clean up the exposure, create a new key, update services, review access) before revoking the affected key. The exposed key must still be revoked, because anyone holding it can send data into your org. Agents have no application-key fallback.

questions.question: Your org uses separate API keys for production Agents, staging Agents and a Terraform pipeline. An admin revokes only the staging key. What is the effect?
choices: Only clients using the staging key have data rejected
All Agents stop, since every org API key shares one secret
The production and Terraform keys are revoked along with it
Nothing changes until the staging Agents are restarted
questions.explanation: Each API key is revoked on its own, so only the Agents and scripts configured with the revoked key have their submissions rejected, while production and Terraform keep working. That isolation is why Datadog suggests a different API key for each deployment method, so one key can be rotated or revoked without affecting the others. Revocation takes effect on Datadog's side within a few seconds, so it doesn't wait for an Agent restart.

questions.question: Which Datadog managed role includes, by default, the API Keys Write permission needed to create API keys?
choices: Datadog Read Only Role
Datadog Standard Role
Datadog Admin Role
questions.explanation: API Keys Write (`api_keys_write`, create and rename API keys) and API Keys Delete default to the Datadog Admin Role. The Standard Role gets API Keys Read (`api_keys_read`), which lists and retrieves API key values, and Read Only gets neither. Managed roles inherit from less powerful roles, so Admin also has the read permission.

questions.question: A user who has only the Datadog Standard Role is installing an Agent and needs an API key. What can they do with the default permissions?
choices: Copy an existing API key's value, but not create a new key
Nothing; only the Datadog Admin Role can see API key values
Both copy existing API keys and create new ones as needed
Nothing; API key values are only shown once, at creation
questions.explanation: The Standard Role has API Keys Read (`api_keys_read`), which lets users list and retrieve the key values of all API keys in the org, while API Keys Write for creating keys defaults to the Admin Role. The show-once behavior applies to application keys (One-Time Read mode and service account keys), not to API keys.

questions.question: The admin who created the API key used by every production Agent leaves the company, and her Datadog account is disabled. What happens to the Agents' data submission?
choices: It continues, because API keys from a disabled account stay valid
It stops at once, because her API keys are revoked with the account
It continues for 7 days, then stops unless the key is restored
It continues only if an admin transfers the key to another user
questions.explanation: When a user account is disabled, API keys that it created are not deleted and remain valid; only the user's application keys are revoked. No transfer is needed because API keys belong to the organization, and there is no grace period or expiry: the key stays valid until someone revokes it.

questions.question: Datadog API and application keys are long-lived credentials. What does Datadog say about their expiration and storage?
choices: They don't expire on their own, so store them in a secrets manager
They expire after 90 days, so rotate them through the Agent config
They expire after one year unless they are used at least monthly
They expire when unused for 30 days, so keep them in source code
questions.explanation: Because API and application keys are long-lived and have no built-in expiration, Datadog recommends storing them in a secrets manager such as AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault or Azure Key Vault instead of in source code or environment files. Rotation is your responsibility; there is no 90-day, yearly or inactivity-based expiry.

questions.question: A CI pipeline creates a new API key and uses it in the very next step. That step sometimes fails with 403 Forbidden, but a rerun a few seconds later succeeds. What explains this?
choices: Key changes are eventually consistent and need a few seconds
New API keys must be approved by an admin before they can be used
New API keys work only after the Agent has been restarted once
The pipeline exceeded the X-RateLimit-Limit for key creation
questions.explanation: Datadog keys follow an eventual consistency model: creation and revocation may take a few seconds to propagate, so using a brand-new key immediately can cause temporary 401 or 403 errors. Datadog recommends a short wait or retries with exponential backoff, and `/api/v1/validate` can confirm the key is usable. A rate limit would return 429, and there is no admin approval step.

questions.question: When a Datadog user account is disabled, what happens to the API keys and application keys that the account created?
choices: API keys remain valid; application keys are revoked
API keys remain valid; application keys pass to the inviting admin
Both the API keys and the application keys are revoked
API keys are revoked; application keys remain valid
questions.explanation: Disabling a user revokes every application key that user created, while API keys created by the account are not deleted and stay valid because they belong to the organization. Datadog never transfers application keys from one user to another for security reasons; use a service account for keys that must outlive an individual.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an application key in Datadog?
choices: It replaces the API key so the Agent can send metrics without one
It lets browser and mobile SDKs send RUM events and logs securely
Paired with an API key, it grants access to the Datadog API
It authenticates DogStatsD clients that send metrics to the Agent
questions.explanation: Application keys, in conjunction with your organization's API key, give users access to Datadog's programmatic API, and by default they carry the permissions of the user who created them. The Agent always sends data with an API key, browser and mobile SDKs use client tokens, and DogStatsD traffic to the local Agent does not use application keys.

questions.question: A user whose role can view but not edit dashboards creates an application key without any scopes. A script using that key tries to delete a dashboard. What happens?
choices: It succeeds, because unscoped keys have full access to the org
It succeeds, because the paired API key grants write access
It is denied, since the key carries only that user's permissions
It succeeds, but only if the request is sent to a v2 endpoint
questions.explanation: If no scopes are specified, an application key has the same scopes and permissions as the user who created it, so a user who cannot delete dashboards cannot do it through their key either. The API key does not add permissions to the call, and the API version does not change authorization.

questions.question: A reporting script only needs to read dashboards. Following Datadog's best practice, how should its application key be set up?
choices: Create it from an Admin account so it never hits permission errors
Skip it; an API key alone is enough to read dashboard definitions
Scope it to only the needed scopes, such as `dashboards_read`
Use a client token instead, because tokens are limited to reads
questions.explanation: Datadog recommends granting application keys the minimal privileges an application needs, and a scoped key gets only the scopes you specify and no other permissions. An unscoped Admin-owned key exposes far more than required. Reading data needs both an API key and an application key, and client tokens are only for browser, mobile and TV clients sending data.

questions.question: A Datadog Admin creates an application key scoped only to `dashboards_read` and hands it to a script. The script then tries to create a monitor. What happens?
choices: It succeeds, because the key's owner has the Admin role
It succeeds, since scopes only restrict reads, not writes
It is denied; the key has only the scopes it was granted
It succeeds once, then the key's scopes expand automatically
questions.explanation: Scoped application keys are granted only the scopes specified and no other additional permissions, even when the owner's role could do more. Scopes limit write operations as well as reads, and they never expand on their own. To let the script create monitors, add the needed scope (such as `monitors_write`) to the key.

questions.question: An application key was scoped to `monitors_read` and `monitors_write`. Later, the role of the user who owns the key is changed. What happens to the scopes on that key?
choices: They are replaced by the new role's permissions
They are cleared, and the key becomes unscoped
They stay exactly as they were set
The key is revoked and must be created again
questions.explanation: Datadog notes that if a user's role or permissions change, the authorization scopes specified for their application keys remain unchanged. A role change does not rescope, clear or revoke the key; disabling the user is what revokes their application keys. If the key needs different access, you can edit its scopes at any time.

questions.question: A nightly automation script calls the Datadog API with an engineer's personal application key. How do you keep it from breaking when that engineer leaves and their account is disabled?
choices: Transfer the engineer's application key to their manager first
Create a service account and use an application key it owns
Switch the script to an API key only, since it never expires
Generate a client token for the script, as it has no owner
questions.explanation: When an account is disabled its application keys are revoked, and Datadog does not transfer application keys between users for security reasons, so it recommends a service account application key for shared automation. An API key alone cannot read data through the API, and client tokens are only for browser, mobile and TV clients.

questions.question: What is a Datadog service account?
choices: A shared UI login that several team members use for on-call work
A special API key that does not count toward the 50-key org limit
A Datadog-managed user that support engineers use to access your org
A non-interactive account that owns app keys and shared resources
questions.explanation: Service accounts are non-interactive accounts used to own application keys and other resources that are shared across teams, so automation doesn't depend on an individual user. They are not shared human logins or a type of API key. The keys that don't count toward the 50-key limit are managed API keys created by Datadog integrations or services.

questions.question: You created an application key for a service account and closed the dialog without copying the secret. What should you do?
choices: Reopen the service account panel to copy the secret
Ask Datadog Support to reveal the key's secret
Retrieve the secret through the Key Management API
Revoke that key and create a new application key
questions.explanation: A service account application key can be viewed exactly once, immediately after it is created; after the dialog closes, its value cannot be retrieved. Datadog's documented fix for a lost or forgotten service account key is to revoke it and create a new one, not to look it up again in the UI or API.

questions.question: Which permission lets a user create service accounts in Datadog?
choices: Org App Keys Write
Service Account Write
User App Keys
API Keys Write
questions.explanation: Creating a service account requires the Service Account Write permission, which the Datadog Admin Role includes. API Keys Write creates org API keys, Org App Keys Write manages application keys owned by any user, and User App Keys covers a user's own application keys. Disabling a service account also requires User Manage Access.

questions.question: A security engineer must find and revoke application keys owned by other users across the organization. Which permission does this require?
choices: `user_app_keys`
`org_app_keys_read`
`service_account_write`
`org_app_keys_write`
questions.explanation: `org_app_keys_write` (Datadog Admin Role by default) manages application keys owned by all users in the organization. `org_app_keys_read` can only view them, `user_app_keys` is limited to the user's own keys, and `service_account_write` covers creating, disabling and using service accounts rather than other users' keys.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts Datadog API keys and application keys?
choices: API keys belong to the org; app keys belong to the user who made them
API keys belong to a user; app keys belong to the whole organization
Both belong to the org, and neither of them carries a user's permissions
Both belong to a user and are revoked when that user is disabled
questions.explanation: API keys are unique to your organization, while application keys are associated with the user account that created them and by default carry that user's permissions. That is why disabling a user revokes the application keys they created but leaves their API keys valid, and why Datadog recommends service accounts to own application keys for shared automation.

questions.question: You enable the Datadog Cluster Agent's external metrics server so the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can scale on Datadog metrics. Besides an API key, what must the Cluster Agent be given?
choices: A client token
An application key
A second API key
Nothing else is needed
questions.explanation: To serve Datadog metrics to the autoscaler, the Cluster Agent has to read metric values from Datadog, and reading data through the Datadog API requires an application key along with the API key. Datadog's setup guide lists a valid API key and application key as requirements (for example `DD_API_KEY` and `DD_APP_KEY`). A second API key adds no read access, and client tokens are only for browser, mobile and TV clients.

questions.question: An hour ago an admin revoked, by mistake, the application key used by a reporting script. What can be done?
choices: Unrevoke the key within 7 days from the Revoked filter
Create a new application key and update the script
Ask the key owner to unrevoke it from their profile
Restore it with the Key Management API within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Revoking an application key is permanent; the 7-day restoration window applies only to API keys. The fix is to create a new application key (ideally owned by a service account, for automation) and update the script to use it.

questions.question: Which description matches the Datadog API?
choices: A GraphQL API that serves every query from a single endpoint
An HTTP REST API with resource-oriented URLs that returns JSON
A gRPC API that exchanges Protocol Buffers messages over HTTP/2
A SOAP web service that exchanges XML documents described by WSDL
questions.explanation: Datadog describes its API as an HTTP REST API that uses resource-oriented URLs, returns JSON from all requests and uses standard HTTP response codes to indicate success or failure. It is not GraphQL, gRPC or SOAP; the cURL examples and official client libraries all call REST endpoints such as `/api/v2/series`.

questions.question: Which HTTP request header carries the API key when you call the Datadog API?
choices: `X-Datadog-Api-Key`
`DD-API-KEY`
`Authorization: Bearer <api-key>`
`DD-APPLICATION-KEY`
questions.explanation: You authenticate with an API key in the `DD-API-KEY` header, and endpoints that also need an application key take it in `DD-APPLICATION-KEY`. `X-Datadog-Api-Key` is not the documented header, and API keys are not sent as bearer tokens. Passing keys as `api_key` query parameters is deprecated in favor of the headers.

questions.question: A partner tool has been given only your organization's API key, with no application key. Which of these API operations can it perform?
choices: Query timeseries with `GET /api/v1/query`
Create a monitor with `POST /api/v1/monitor`
Post an event with `POST /api/v1/events`
List active metrics with `GET /api/v1/metrics`
questions.explanation: Endpoints that write data, such as posting events, submitting metrics or submitting service checks, require only an API key. Querying timeseries, listing active metrics and creating monitors read data or manage resources, so they also require an application key in the `DD-APPLICATION-KEY` header.

questions.question: According to Datadog's API authentication rules, which requests need an application key in addition to the API key?
choices: Requests that write data
Requests that read data
Requests sent to the EU site
Requests with gzip-compressed bodies
questions.explanation: Datadog states that all API requests must be authenticated: requests that write data require an API key, while requests that read data require full access and also an application key. The site you call and whether the body is compressed don't change which keys are needed.

questions.question: A nightly batch job runs on a server that has no Datadog Agent installed. It must send a custom metric straight to Datadog over HTTPS. Which should it use?
choices: DogStatsD
A custom Agent check
The Datadog API
The Datadog Agent
questions.explanation: Custom metrics can be submitted through a custom Agent check, DogStatsD or the HTTP API, among other ways, but of these options only the API (for example `POST /api/v2/series` with an API key) accepts metrics directly over HTTPS without an Agent. DogStatsD clients send datagrams to the DogStatsD server built into the Agent, and custom checks run inside the Agent.

questions.question: Your organization's Datadog UI is at `https://app.datadoghq.eu`. Which base URL should your API calls use?
choices: `https://api.datadoghq.com`
`https://api.datadoghq.eu`
`https://eu.api.datadoghq.com`
`https://api.eu1.datadoghq.com`
questions.explanation: Each Datadog site has its own API host; for EU1 (`app.datadoghq.eu`, site parameter `datadoghq.eu`) the endpoints are under `https://api.datadoghq.eu`. `api.datadoghq.com` is the US1 host, and because sites are completely independent, an EU org's keys don't work there. The `eu.api` and `api.eu1` hostnames are not Datadog endpoints.

questions.question: Your team logs in to Datadog at `https://us3.datadoghq.com`. A script posts metrics to `https://api.datadoghq.com/api/v2/series` and gets 403 errors even though the key is valid in your org. Which URL should it use?
choices: `https://us3.api.datadoghq.com/api/v2/series`
`https://api.datadoghq.com/us3/api/v2/series`
`https://api.us3.datadoghq.com/api/v2/series`
`https://us3.datadoghq.com/intake/api/v2/series`
questions.explanation: API hosts follow the site: US3 (`us3.datadoghq.com`) uses `https://api.us3.datadoghq.com`, while `api.datadoghq.com` belongs to US1. Datadog sites are completely independent, so a US3 org's key is rejected with an authentication error on US1. The other hostnames and paths are not valid Datadog endpoints.

questions.question: A `POST /api/v2/series` request returns HTTP 202 with the body `{"errors": []}`. What does this mean?
choices: The payload was accepted and will be processed
The request was queued because of rate limiting
The key was valid, but the points were discarded
The request must be retried with an application key
questions.explanation: For the Submit metrics endpoint, 202 means Payload accepted, and the v2 example response is an empty `errors` list. Rate limiting returns 429 and authentication problems return 403. Metric submission needs only an API key, so an application key is never the issue.

questions.question: A script that submits metrics to `/api/v2/series` suddenly starts receiving HTTP 403 responses. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The JSON body is malformed or has a wrong field type
The API key in `DD-API-KEY` is invalid or missing
The payload is over the endpoint's maximum size
The script is sending too many requests per second
questions.explanation: The Submit metrics endpoint documents 403 as an authentication error, which points to a missing, revoked or wrong-site API key. A malformed body returns 400 Bad Request, an oversized payload returns 413 Payload Too Large and excessive requests return 429 Too Many Requests.

questions.question: An exporter batches thousands of series into one uncompressed `POST /api/v2/series` request and receives HTTP 413. What should it change?
choices: Add an application key header to raise the size limit
Wait for the X-RateLimit-Reset period before retrying
Split the data into smaller requests under 500 KB each
Switch the timestamps from seconds to milliseconds
questions.explanation: 413 means Payload too large. The v2 endpoint accepts at most 500 kilobytes (512000 bytes) per payload, and compressed payloads must decompress to less than 5 megabytes, so the fix is smaller batches (compression also helps). An application key doesn't change limits, 429 is the rate-limit response, and timestamps must stay in seconds.

questions.question: What is the maximum payload size for a single request to the v2 Submit metrics endpoint, `POST /api/v2/series`?
choices: 3.2 megabytes (3200000 bytes)
5 megabytes (5242880 bytes)
500 kilobytes (512000 bytes)
62 megabytes (62914560 bytes)
questions.explanation: The v2 endpoint's maximum payload size is 500 kilobytes (512000 bytes), and compressed payloads must have a decompressed size of less than 5 megabytes (5242880 bytes). The 3.2 MB limit, with its 62 MB decompressed ceiling, belongs to the older v1 endpoint `POST /api/v1/series`.

questions.question: A job uses `POST /api/v2/series` to backfill metric points whose timestamps are three hours old. Which documented rule does this break?
choices: Points may be no more than 10 minutes in the past
Points must be sent with millisecond timestamps
Backfilling requires an application key as well
Points may be no more than 1 hour in the past
questions.explanation: Metric point timestamps must be POSIX time in seconds and current, meaning no more than 10 minutes in the future or 1 hour in the past. Ten minutes is the future limit, not the past one, and adding an application key does not widen the window.

questions.question: A script polling monitor status receives HTTP 429. Which response header tells it how many seconds remain until the rate limit resets?
choices: `X-RateLimit-Reset`
`X-RateLimit-Period`
`X-RateLimit-Remaining`
`X-RateLimit-Limit`
questions.explanation: `X-RateLimit-Reset` is the time in seconds until the next reset. `X-RateLimit-Period` is the length of the calendar-aligned period, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` is how many requests are left in the current period, and `X-RateLimit-Limit` is how many requests are allowed per period.

questions.question: A team plans to send very high volumes of points through the Metrics API and asks how Datadog rate limits metric submission. What does Datadog document?
choices: It is capped at 250,000 points per minute per organization
It is not rate limited; custom metric volume drives billing
It follows per-endpoint limits shown in the X-RateLimit headers
It is capped at 1,000 requests per hour for each API key
questions.explanation: Datadog does not rate limit data point or metric submission; what you run into depends on your custom metrics volume under your agreement, and usage beyond your allotment is billed. 250,000 per minute per organization is the event submission limit. Other endpoints have limits reported in X-RateLimit headers.

questions.question: Before rolling an API key out to new Agents, you want to confirm it is valid. You don't have an application key. Which request should you make?
choices: `GET /api/v2/validate_keys`
`GET /api/v1/metrics`
`GET /api/v1/validate`
`GET /api/v1/query`
questions.explanation: `GET /api/v1/validate` checks whether the API key (not the application key) is valid using only `DD-API-KEY`, returning `{"valid": true}` or a 403. `/api/v2/validate_keys` checks an API key and application key pair, so it needs both. Listing active metrics and querying timeseries read data and also require an application key.

questions.question: Which Datadog API endpoint queries timeseries data across various data sources and lets you process it with formulas and functions?
choices: `POST /api/v2/series`
`POST /api/v2/query/timeseries`
`GET /api/v2/metrics/{metric_name}/all-tags`
`GET /api/v1/metrics`
questions.explanation: `POST /api/v2/query/timeseries` queries timeseries data across various data sources and processes it by applying formulas and functions; current docs also recommend it over the older `GET /api/v1/query`. `POST /api/v2/series` submits metrics, `GET /api/v1/metrics` lists actively reporting metrics, and the `all-tags` endpoint lists tags for one metric.

questions.question:
This request returns HTTP 403 even though the API key is valid:

curl -X GET "https://api.datadoghq.com/api/v1/query?from=1700000000&to=1700003600&query=avg:system.cpu.user{*}" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -H "DD-API-KEY: ${DD_API_KEY}"

What is the most likely fix?
choices: Change the request method to POST
Send `from` and `to` in milliseconds
Add the `DD-APPLICATION-KEY` header
Move the API key into an `api_key` query parameter
questions.explanation: Query timeseries points reads data, so it requires both `DD-API-KEY` and `DD-APPLICATION-KEY`; without the application key the request is refused. The v1 query endpoint is a GET with `from` and `to` in seconds since the Unix epoch, and moving the API key into a (deprecated) query parameter would not supply the missing application key.

choices: `POST /api/v1/series`
`POST /api/v1/distribution_points`
`POST /api/v2/query/timeseries`
`POST /api/v2/series`
questions.explanation: The v2 Submit metrics format uses point objects with `timestamp` and `value`, a numeric `type` (0 unspecified, 1 count, 2 rate, 3 gauge) and a `resources` list that names the host. The v1 format sends points as `[timestamp, value]` tuples with a `host` field and a string type such as `gauge`. Distribution points and the timeseries query endpoint use different payloads.

questions.question: By default, which environment variables do Datadog's official API client libraries, such as the Python and TypeScript `datadog-api-client` packages, read for authentication?
choices: `DD-API-KEY` and `DD-APPLICATION-KEY`
`DD_API_KEY` and `DD_APP_KEY`
`DD_API_KEY` and `DD_CLIENT_TOKEN`
`DD_SITE` and `DD_HOSTNAME`
questions.explanation: The official client libraries use the `DD_API_KEY` and `DD_APP_KEY` environment variables by default to authenticate against the Datadog API. `DD-API-KEY` and `DD-APPLICATION-KEY` are the HTTP header names, not environment variables. Client tokens are for browser and mobile SDKs, and `DD_SITE` and `DD_HOSTNAME` are not credentials.

questions.question: A Python script built on the official Datadog API client works for a US1 org, but it gets 403 errors when run with keys from an EU1 org. What is the fix?
choices: Create new EU-specific keys in the US1 org
Point the client at `https://api.datadoghq.eu`
Add an `X-Datadog-Region: eu1` header to requests
Use a client token, since keys are US-only
questions.explanation: Datadog API clients target the US site by default, and sites are fully independent, so EU keys aren't recognized by the US1 API. Configure the client for the EU site so it calls `https://api.datadoghq.eu`; in the Python client, set `configuration.server_variables["site"] = "datadoghq.eu"` or the `DD_SITE` environment variable. There is no region header, and client tokens don't authenticate API calls.

questions.question: A team uses an official Datadog API client from an EU organization but leaves the client at its default US site. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Switch DogStatsD from UDP to TCP
Regenerate the hostnames for all monitored systems
Set the client host or site for the correct Datadog region
Move the dashboard into the Host Map view
questions.explanation: Official Datadog API clients default to the US site unless configured otherwise. If your organization is on another site, you must point the client at the correct Datadog host so requests reach the right regional API.

questions.question: Which Datadog API area would you use to submit a custom metric directly over HTTP?
choices: The metrics endpoint
The host map endpoint
Only the authentication settings page
The monitor mute endpoint
questions.explanation: Datadog's API includes metrics endpoints for programmatically submitting metric data. That is a direct alternative when you are not sending custom metrics through DogStatsD or an Agent-based check.

questions.question: An organization uses the Datadog EU site. What must be configured correctly on the Agent or API client?
choices: The Windows desktop theme
A local SMTP relay
The shell prompt color
The correct Datadog site or API host, such as datadoghq.eu
questions.explanation: Datadog accounts are tied to specific sites, and the Agent or API client must be pointed at the correct one. If the site is wrong, data and API calls may go to the wrong intake or fail entirely.

questions.question: One-Time Read mode is enabled for application keys. What should an engineer expect when creating a new application key?
choices: The key can only be used over DogStatsD on port 8125
The secret automatically becomes an API key after an Agent restart
The secret is shown once at creation time and should be stored immediately
The secret can be viewed later by any admin in plain text
questions.explanation: Datadog's One-Time Read behavior means the application key secret is only displayed when the key is created. If you do not store it securely at that moment, you cannot retrieve the secret later and must create a new key.

questions.question: If you cannot run the Agent but still need to submit a custom metric directly to Datadog, which public API area should you use?
choices: The Monitors Search API
The SAML settings API
The Host Map API
The Metrics submission API, such as the series endpoint
questions.explanation: Datadog exposes public intake endpoints for metrics, logs, events, and traces when Agent-based collection is not the right fit. For custom metrics, the metrics submission endpoint is the relevant API family.

questions.question: An organization uses the EU1 Datadog site. Which site parameter should the Agent or API client use?
choices: us3.datadoghq.com
ddog-gov.com
datadoghq.com
datadoghq.eu
questions.explanation: The site parameter must match the Datadog site your organization actually uses. EU1 uses `datadoghq.eu`, not the default US site.

questions.question: A team automates Datadog resource creation with Terraform. Which credential pair does the provider typically need?
choices: A SAML assertion and a browser cookie
An SSH key and a hostname
A client token and a DogStatsD port
An API key and an application key with sufficient permissions
questions.explanation: The Datadog Terraform provider authenticates with an API key and an application key associated with a user or service account that has the required permissions. The API key identifies the organization and the application key authorizes the API operations the provider performs.

questions.question: What is an application key primarily used for in Datadog?
choices: Replacing the host hostname
Enabling DogStatsD on port 8125
Calling the Datadog programmatic API together with an API key
Encrypting telemetry inside the Agent
questions.explanation: Datadog's programmatic API uses an API key plus an application key for user-level access. The Agent itself does not need an application key just to forward host data.

questions.question: A script needs to create dashboards through the Datadog API. Which credential set is typically required?
choices: Only an API key
An API key plus an application key
Only an application key
No credentials if the script runs on a private network
questions.explanation: Most Datadog API actions that manage resources require an API key and an application key together. The API key identifies the organization, while the application key provides the caller's authorized API access.

questions.question: Why do teams often prefer a service account application key for automation instead of a personal user's key?
choices: It forces all automation to run from the UI
It avoids tying critical automation to one employee's account lifecycle
It automatically scopes requests to one host only
It removes the need for an API key on requests
questions.explanation: Service account keys survive personnel changes more cleanly than personal keys. That reduces surprise outages when a user's role or account changes.

questions.question: Why should a browser-based application not use a Datadog API key directly?
choices: Because API keys work only over UDP
Because API keys can create dashboards only from Linux
Because browsers cannot make HTTPS requests to Datadog
Because the key would be exposed client-side; end-user apps should use client tokens instead
questions.explanation: Datadog API keys are sensitive credentials and should not be embedded in code that runs on a user's device. For browser, mobile, and similar end-user applications, Datadog provides client tokens for the supported telemetry products.

questions.question: Which key is used together with an API key to access Datadog's programmatic management APIs?
choices: Windows registry key
Application key
SSH key
DogStatsD key
questions.explanation: Application keys are paired with an organization's API key for authenticated access to many Datadog API operations. They are associated with a user or service account and inherit allowed scopes or permissions.

questions.question: Why is a service account application key usually safer for shared automation than a personal application key?
choices: It replaces the need for an API key
It can be embedded safely in browser JavaScript
It avoids breaking automation when the employee who created the key is deactivated
It makes the Datadog site parameter unnecessary
questions.explanation: Application keys created by individual users are tied to those user accounts. If that person is disabled, their application keys are revoked, so shared automation is more durable when it uses a service account instead.

questions.question: A Datadog API key is stored in a configuration file. Which file-permission approach best follows least privilege?
choices: Make the file executable by all users
Place the file in a publicly accessible web directory
Make the file world-writable so any user can edit it
Allow read and write access only to the required service or administrator accounts
questions.explanation: Least privilege means only the users or services that truly need access should have it. Configuration files that contain secrets should not be writable or readable by everyone on the system.

questions.question: Which credential must a Datadog Agent have to submit metrics and events to your Datadog organization?
choices: Application key
API key
SAML assertion
Client token
questions.explanation: API keys are organization-level credentials used by the Agent for telemetry intake. Application keys are for programmatic API access, not basic Agent data submission.

questions.question: A user who created both API keys and application keys is deactivated. What happens by default?
choices: Application keys are revoked, but API keys created by that user remain valid
Both API keys and application keys are automatically deleted
API keys are revoked, but application keys remain valid
Nothing changes until Support is contacted
questions.explanation: Application keys are tied to the creating user, so disabling that user revokes those keys. API keys are organization-level intake credentials, so keys created by that account are not automatically deleted and remain valid until you revoke them.

questions.question: Why might an organization deliberately create multiple Datadog API keys instead of sharing one everywhere?
choices: Each dashboard requires its own API key
It increases metric retention automatically
It makes rotation and revocation easier for specific deployments
Application keys stop working without it
questions.explanation: Datadog recommends considering multiple API keys for different deployment methods or services. That makes key rotation safer and lets you revoke a compromised or retired key without breaking every Agent and automation workflow at once.

questions.question: Which credential must the Datadog Agent have to submit metrics and events to Datadog?
choices: API key
Application key
OAuth redirect URI
SSH public key
questions.explanation: The Datadog Agent uses an API key to send telemetry data into your Datadog organization. Application keys are for authenticated programmatic access to many API endpoints, not basic Agent submission.

questions.question: Which approach is Datadog's recommended method for managing dashboards, monitors, and integrations as code in a version-controlled workflow?
choices: Storing dashboards as screenshots in object storage
Exporting browser cookies into a git repository
Editing YAML files on each host manually
Using the Datadog Terraform provider to declare and apply resources
questions.explanation: Datadog publishes an official Terraform provider that lets teams declare dashboards, monitors, synthetic tests, and other resources as code. Applying Terraform keeps configuration version-controlled and repeatable across environments.

questions.question: To read data from many Datadog API endpoints programmatically, which credentials are typically required?
choices: Hostname and DogStatsD port
Application key only
API key only
Both an API key and an application key
questions.explanation: Write operations require an API key, and many read operations also require an application key associated with a user or service account that has the needed permissions. Together, the key pair authenticates the client and authorizes access to the endpoint.

questions.question: Right after creating a new API key, an automation job fails for a few seconds before succeeding. What is the best explanation?
choices: Application keys are required for all DogStatsD traffic
New Datadog keys only work during business hours
API keys must be activated by restarting the Agent service
Datadog key changes are eventually consistent and may take a few seconds to propagate
questions.explanation: Datadog documents a short propagation delay for API and application key creation or revocation. Short retries with backoff or use of the validation endpoints are the right response to that brief consistency window.

questions.question: An EU-based organization's host Agent shows healthy local checks, but no fresh data reaches the Datadog site after install. Which misconfiguration is a strong suspect?
choices: The host uses too many dashboard widgets
The host has more than one CPU core
The `DD_SITE` or site setting still points to the wrong Datadog site
The application key has more permissions than the API key
questions.explanation: A host can look healthy locally while still sending to the wrong intake site. If an EU organization points at the US default site, data may not land where the team expects.

questions.question: Which credential is required by the Datadog Agent to submit metrics and events to your organization?
choices: Client token
OAuth refresh token
Application key
API key
questions.explanation: API keys are organization-scoped and are required for Agents to send metrics and events. Application keys serve a different purpose: authenticated API access on behalf of a user or service account.

questions.question: Which statement about Datadog application keys is correct?
choices: They are automatically shared across all organizations
They are never associated with a user or service account
They are required for the Agent to submit metrics and events
They are used with an API key to access Datadog's programmatic API
questions.explanation: Application keys are used alongside an organization's API key for many Datadog API actions. They are tied to a user or service account context, which is why they are different from organization-wide API keys used for intake.

flashcards.front: What is a Datadog API key used for?
flashcards.back: An organization-level key that the Datadog Agent requires to submit metrics and events. API keys are unique to your organization and are sent in the DD-API-KEY header on API calls; requests that only write data need nothing else.

flashcards.front: How do you give the Agent its API key?
flashcards.back: Set `api_key` in datadog.yaml (a required setting), or set the DD_API_KEY environment variable, for example for containerized Agents.

flashcards.front: API key limits per organization
flashcards.back: At least one API key is required, and up to 50 are allowed by default (Support can raise the limit). Managed API keys created by integrations don't count. Key names must be unique across the org.

flashcards.front: What happens to API keys when the user who created them is disabled?
flashcards.back: Nothing: they are not deleted and stay valid. Only that user's application keys are revoked. Client tokens they created also stay active.

flashcards.front: Client token vs. API key
flashcards.back: Client tokens are for end-user-facing apps (browser, Android, iOS, React Native, Flutter and Roku log collectors; RUM), because an API key would be exposed client-side. Both are unique to your organization.

flashcards.front: Can a revoked API key be restored?
flashcards.back: Current behavior (documented in 2026): yes, within 7 days. Filter the API Keys tab by Revoked status and click Unrevoke (UI only, no API). The key comes back with the same name, ID and value. Removed client tokens can't be recovered.

flashcards.front: Steps after an API or application key is exposed
flashcards.back:
1. Revoke the key (if usage is large or unknown, do steps 2-5 first)
2. Remove it from public files and commit history
3. Create a new key
4. Update affected services
5. Review the account for new users, new resources and role changes

flashcards.front: API key permissions and their default roles
flashcards.back:
api_keys_read: list and retrieve key values (Standard Role)
api_keys_write: create and rename keys (Admin Role)
api_keys_delete: delete keys (Admin Role)

flashcards.front: Why use multiple API keys?
flashcards.back: Using one key per deployment method (for example Kubernetes in AWS, Chef on-prem, Terraform, local dev) lets you rotate a key, or revoke one that was exposed or retired, without affecting the others.

flashcards.front: Do Datadog API keys expire, and how quickly do key changes take effect?
flashcards.back: They don't expire: API and application keys are long-lived with no built-in expiration, so store them in a secrets manager and rotate them yourself. Creating or revoking a key is eventually consistent and can take a few seconds to propagate.

flashcards.front: What is an application key?
flashcards.back: A key used together with an API key (DD-APPLICATION-KEY header) for programmatic access to the Datadog API, such as reading data. It belongs to the user or service account that created it and, if unscoped, has that owner's permissions.

flashcards.front: Application key scopes
flashcards.back: Optional authorization scopes limit a key to the listed scopes only, with no other permissions (least privilege). Scope names are case-sensitive. Scopes stay the same if the owner's role changes. Unscoped keys get all of the owner's permissions.

flashcards.front: What happens to application keys when their owner is disabled?
flashcards.back: They are revoked. Datadog does not transfer application keys between users, so use a service account for keys that must outlive a person.

flashcards.front: What is a service account?
flashcards.back: A non-interactive account that owns application keys and other shared resources, so automation keeps working when people leave. Creating one requires Service Account Write (included in the Admin Role), and it can get any subset of your own roles.

flashcards.front: When can you see a service account application key's secret?
flashcards.back: Only once, right after you create it. If it is lost, revoke it and create a new key.

flashcards.front: One-Time Read (OTR) mode
flashcards.back: A security setting introduced in August 2025 (current behavior): application key secrets are shown once, at creation, and can't be retrieved later through the UI or API. OTR is on permanently for new parent orgs created after August 20, 2025. Existing orgs can toggle it for 3 months, after which it becomes permanent (toggling requires org_app_keys_write and org_management).

flashcards.front: Application key permissions and their default roles
flashcards.back:
user_app_keys: view and manage your own keys (Standard Role)
org_app_keys_read: view all users' keys (Standard Role)
org_app_keys_write: manage all users' keys (Admin Role)

flashcards.front: Can a revoked application key be restored?
flashcards.back: No. Revoking an application key is permanent, so create a new key and update whatever used the old one. (Current docs add a 7-day unrevoke window for API keys only.)

flashcards.front: Actions API access on an application key
flashcards.back: Current behavior (added in 2025): it must be enabled, in the UI or through the API, before the key can call the App Builder, Actions Connections or Workflow Automation APIs. By default, application keys can't use these APIs.

flashcards.front: Datadog API authentication headers
flashcards.back:
DD-API-KEY: the API key (every key-authenticated request)
DD-APPLICATION-KEY: the application key (endpoints that read data or manage resources, such as queries and monitors)

flashcards.front: Which requests need only an API key, and which need both keys?
flashcards.back:
API key only: writing data, such as POST /api/v2/series, POST /api/v1/events and POST /api/v1/check_run, plus GET /api/v1/validate.
API key + application key: reading data, such as GET /api/v1/query and GET /api/v1/metrics.

flashcards.front: API base URL for each Datadog site
flashcards.back:
US1: api.datadoghq.com
US3: api.us3.datadoghq.com
US5: api.us5.datadoghq.com
EU1: api.datadoghq.eu
AP1: api.ap1.datadoghq.com
AP2: api.ap2.datadoghq.com
UK1: api.uk1.datadoghq.com
US1-FED: api.ddog-gov.com
US2-FED: api.us2.ddog-gov.com

flashcards.front: Metric submission endpoints and their payload limits
flashcards.back:
v2, POST /api/v2/series: at most 500 KB (512000 bytes), and compressed payloads must decompress to under 5 MB (5242880 bytes).
v1, POST /api/v1/series: at most 3.2 MB (3200000 bytes), and under 62 MB decompressed.

flashcards.front: Timestamp rules for submitted metric points
flashcards.back: POSIX time in seconds, and current: no more than 10 minutes in the future or 1 hour in the past.

flashcards.front: Response codes for Submit metrics
flashcards.back:
202 Payload accepted
400 Bad Request
403 Authentication error
408 Request timeout
413 Payload too large
429 Too many requests

flashcards.front: The X-RateLimit-* response headers
flashcards.back:
Limit: requests allowed per period
Period: period length in seconds (calendar aligned)
Remaining: requests left in the current period
Reset: seconds until the next reset
Name: name of the limit, for increase requests

flashcards.front: Which Datadog APIs are rate limited?
flashcards.back: Metric (data point) submission and log submission are not rate limited; metric volume is governed by custom metric billing. Event submission is limited to 250,000 events per minute per org. Other endpoints report their limits in X-RateLimit headers and return 429 when you exceed them.

flashcards.front: How do you validate an API key?
flashcards.back: Call GET /api/v1/validate with only the DD-API-KEY header. It returns {"valid": true}, or 403 if the key is invalid. To check an API key and application key pair, use GET /api/v2/validate_keys.

flashcards.front: Metric `type` values in a v2 series payload
flashcards.back: 0 = unspecified, 1 = count, 2 = rate, 3 = gauge. The v1 API uses strings instead: "", count, gauge, rate.

flashcards.front: How do you query metrics through the API?
flashcards.back: GET /api/v1/query (from and to in epoch seconds, plus query), or POST /api/v2/query/timeseries, which supports formulas and functions across data sources (current docs recommend the v2 endpoint). Both need an API key and an application key.

flashcards.front: Official Datadog API client libraries
flashcards.back: datadog-api-client for Java, Python, Ruby, Go, TypeScript and Rust. Clients target the US site by default; for EU, configure the site as datadoghq.eu (the Python and Rust clients also read DD_SITE). The Python, TypeScript and Rust clients read DD_API_KEY and DD_APP_KEY by default.

flashcards.front: Content-Encoding options for POST /api/v2/series
flashcards.back: deflate (the default), zstd1 or gzip. The v1 /api/v1/series endpoint accepts deflate or gzip.
